AN ACT to amend the social services law and the abandoned property law, in
relation to the transfer of unclaimed support collections and unidentified
payments; and repealing certain provisions of such laws relating thereto
items.lawCode: Rpld §111-h subs 5 - 7 & 12 - 17, amd §111-h, Soc Serv L; rpld §600 sub 1 ¶(c), §602 sub 3, add §1318, Ab Prop L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S7153

SPONSOR: KRUEGER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the social services law and the abandoned property law,
in relation to the transfer of unclaimed support collections and uniden-
tified payments; and repealing certain provisions of such laws relating
thereto

 
PURPOSE OF THE BILL:

This bill would clarify and simplify the process by which the support
collection unit (SCU) transfers undisbursed funds to the State Comp-
troller's Office of Unclaimed Funds.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill would amend Social Services Law (SSL) § 111-h by
repealing subdivisions 5-7 and 12-17, renumbering existing subdivisions
18-20 as subdivisions 12-14, and adding new subdivisions 5-7 to allow
for a streamlined administrative procedure utilizing the functions and
capabilities of the automated child support system Which is compliant
with mandatory federal distribution rules governing the disbursement of
support collections. Additionally, the bill would repeal an obsolete
one-time review and adjustment process for orders issued prior to
September 15,1989.

Sections 2 and 3 of the bill would repeal Abandoned Property Law (APL)

§§ 600(1)(c) and 602(3), respectively, both of which are obsolete
provisions of the APL which apply to the support bureau of the Family
Court.

Section 4 of the bill would add APL § 1318, which states that funds
delivered to the State Comptroller pursuant to SSL § 11 1-h (7) would be
deemed abandoned property.

Section 5 of the bill would provide for an immediate effective date,
provided that any funds which were previously deposited with the county
treasurer or the. Commissioner of Finance of the City of New York prior
to the effective date of this act would be delivered to the Office of
the State Comptroller (OSC) no later than April 2022, in accordance with
the newly-enacted SSL § 111-h(7).

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The bill would remove the requirement to make an application to the
Family Court and would require two years of diligent efforts to locate
submitted in accordance with Assembly Rule HI, Sec 1(1) the individual
entitled to the funds collected in cases in which the funds have been
identified with a specific individual's account. In cases where a
payment has been received for which there is inadequate information to
attribute the funds to a specific account, or where the funds are owed
to an individual who is deceased, there would be no requirement to wait
two years before transferring the funds to OSC. These exceptions to the
two-year diligent effort rule would transfer funds to OSC sooner in
these limited situations where additional time and effort are unlikely
to result in greater distribution directly to the individual entitled to
the funds or where the use of additional resources to distribute the
funds is deemed inefficient.

Enactment of this bill would benefit parents by enhancing their abili-
ties to claim child support payments or Overpayments due by utilizing
the established public claims process available on the OSC website.
Additionally, for social services districts that have regularly trans-
ferred undistributed- child support as unclaimed funds, the bill would
provide administrative relief through the simplification of the process.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New Bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

It is estimated that in April 2020, a one-time sum of approximately $7.5
million of current undistributed collections may be payable to OSC as
unclaimed funds and included in the annual sweep by OSC to the State
General Fund pursuant to State Finance Law § 95. The Federal Government
would receive 66 percent of that amount because undistributed
collections must be claimed as program income at the time funds are
transferred to OSC. This would result in a net one-time revenue stream
for the State of approximately $2.6 million.  If the bill is-enacted, it
is possible that, thereafter, an estimated $1 million annually could
potentially be transferred to OSC as abandoned funds - and ultimately
swept to the State General Fund - depending upon the number of claims to
the funds received from owners that ultimately succeed. After accounting
for the 66 percent federal share, this would result in a net recurring
revenue stream for the State of approximately $340,000.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
The bill provides for an immediate effective date, provided that any
funds which were previously deposited with the county treasurer or the
Commissioner of Finance of the City of New York prior to the effective
date of this act would be delivered to OSC no later than April 2022, in
accordance with the newly enacted SSL § 111-h(7).

summary: Provides that any funds paid to a support collection unit which have not been disbursed after two years of diligent efforts to locate the person entitled to such funds, and funds which the remitter of such funds has not provided sufficient identifying information to associate the funds with an existing account shall be paid to the state comptroller.
